newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Growing gold gap seen filled by hedges, bank sales.
newsitem.headline: Growing gold gap seen filled by hedges, bank sales.

text.p: The increasing "gold gap" between supply and demand will continue to be filled by hedging and central bank sales, a leading gold analyst said at a mining conference on Monday.

"What we see is an increasing gold gap. The gap that has been filled over the last 10 years will be over the next 10 years, on an annual basis, about 100 tonnes higher," Rhona O'Connell, founding partner of T.Hoare & Co, told the E.W. Balderson South African mining conference.

O'Connell said 1997's gold gap would likely be 420 tonnes and that this would increase by an average 100 tonnes a year over the next decade, although the gap would really take off after the new millennium.

This gap offered the mining industry scope to hedge an annual 200 tonnes of gold on average and offered central banks the scope to sell almost 300 tonnes of gold a year directly to the market to keep it in balance, O'Connell said.

"There is scope in the mining industry for annual hedging into the market of 220 tonnes and then, should the desire be there, there is scope for central banks to feed almost 300 tonnes into the market to keep the balance," she said.
"There is scope for the gap to be filled."

O'Connell said her hedging outlook was taken from historical numbers which showed that on average roughly 8.5 percent of annual production was hedged each year. According to Gold Fields Mineral Services 1997 Gold report, mine production in 1996 was 2,346 tonnes of gold.

O'Connell did not see much more mine hedging in the future except for some possible panic hedging, especially from Australian producers in the wake of that country's central bank announcement that it had sold two-thirds of its gold reserves.

The Australian central bank announced in early July it had sold 167 tonnes of its gold reserves over the last six months, sending tremors through the world bullion market and knocking the gold price to 12-year lows. It touched $313.60 on July 7.
"The Australian gold sales, or rather the announcement (thereof) sent an unhappy signal to the market, it being the third largest gold producer in the world," O'Connell said.

She said that selling gold one year forward would lock in a price of $330-$332 an ounce, depending on varying interest rates and currency exchange rates. The metal was last trading in London at $325.50/80 an ounce.
"There is a 50-50 chance that by the end of the year it will be at $350 an ounce, but not much higher," O'Connell said, declining to give any further outlook on the gold price.

Central bank sales of gold were an intrinsic part of the market and should not be viewed as a "big ogre", she said. Nor was the market likely to suffer a flurry of central bank sales in the near-term, she said.
O'Connell said that since 1987 the official sector has added 2,200 tonnes of gold to market, of which about 74 percent came from Dutch, Belgian and Canadian sales.
In other words, the remaining 25 percent -- 56 tonnes -- is what has been sold directly by central banks over the last 10 years, she added.

"(Central bank) lending developments have in many cases been critical to the survival of the mining industry. As lenders, the central banks have been facilitators of hedging activity in the traditional mining sector," she said.
O'Connell said she held a cautious view on physical offtake in the Far East over the next five years.
"It will remain the mainstay of the market but it will not grow at the same rate as it did in the 1980s," she said.
As financial markets like bonds and stocks became more developed in the Far East, so investors did not regard gold as quite the same investment they had previously, O'Connell said.
